newsitem.title: CHINA: Beijing fights uphill battle against drug abuse.
newsitem.headline: Beijing fights uphill battle against drug abuse.

text.p: Beijing police have arrested thousands of people for drug-related crimes in the last five years in a resurgence of an addiction once so rampant that China was known as the "Sick Man of East Asia".

Authorities in the Chinese capital have recorded more than 500 cases of drug trafficking and 1,400 cases of drug abuse since 1992, Beijing deputy police chief Ruan Zengyi told a news conference on Wednesday during a rare tour of a drug rehabilitation centre.
During those five years, police rounded up more than 4,000 people who were sternly punished, Ruan said, but gave no figure for the number of drug traffickers who were executed.
China frequently executes drug traffickers as the ultimate deterrent in its war against drugs.
In the past five years, Beijing police seized 213 kg (470 lb) of narcotics, including 58 kg (128 lb) of heroin and 18 kg (40 lb) of ice, or amphetamines, Ruan said.
"We...are fighting a people's war to suppress drugs," he said. "The dying embers of the drug problem are glowing again."
Eighty-nine percent of people arrested by Beijing police for drug crimes were aged below 35, and 87.5 percent were first-time offenders, the deputy police chief said.
China became known as the "Sick Man of East Asia" during the 19th century and first half of this century when opium addiction was widespread.
"In the past, big Western powers used opium and cannons to make the Chinese nation bear (the name) 'Sick Man of East Asia" for more than 100 years," Ruan said.

He was referring to the 19th century Opium Wars when Britain fought to open China to foreign trade. One of the only goods the traders had that Chinese wanted was opium from Britain's colonies in South Asia.
After the communists came to power in 1949, drug abuse was virtually eliminated but has staged a comeback in the past two decades as economic reforms have loosened social controls.
The Chinese capital may have won many battles against drugs, but the war was far from over, officials said.
"Beijing has to a certain degree controlled the spread of drugs, but (the incidence of) drug crimes has increased and the trend is worsening day by day," Ruan said.
The period up to the turn of the century was critical, he said.
"Drug abuse...is a major political problem that is related to social stability, national security and the rise or fall of the nation," the deputy police chief said.
Foreign reporters toured a drug rehabilitation centre in Fangshan county in suburban Beijing and had a rare glimpse of addicts forced to undergo rehabilitation.
A 38-year-old man, surnamed Liu, said the authorities forced him to undergo rehabilitation after he spent all his savings on heroin and his wife reported him to the police.
"In the beginning I hated her for it, but not anymore," said Liu, former owner of a car repair shop.
Gao, a 40-year-old former restaurateur, said drugs could still tempt him even if he were discharged.
Police, acting on a tip-off that he and his wife were addicts, broke into their Beijing home in March, arrested them and forced them to undergo rehabilitation.
China regularly forces addicts to undergo rehabilitation in its bid to curb the spreading abuse of narcotics.
